syllabusTopics: IUPAC Nomenclature of Organic Compounds (up to chain having 6-carbon atoms)
Qualitative analysis of organic compounds (detection of N, S and halogens by Lassaigne's test)

Concept of geometrical isomerism (cis and trans) and optical isomerism (d and l form)
Preliminary idea of reaction mechanism: homolytic and heterolytic fission

rows.text: **Lassaigne's test** makes covalently bound N, S and halogens detectable by one stroke: fuse the compound with **sodium metal** red-hot, drop the mass into water, boil and filter — the **extract** now holds **NaCN, Na₂S and NaX**. **Nitrogen:** FeSO₄ + NaOH builds sodium ferrocyanide; acidification with Fe³⁺ throws **Prussian blue Fe₄[Fe(CN)₆]₃** — unless sulphur is also present, in which case **NaSCN** forms and…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Lassaigne's test detects nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in organic compounds by converting them into ionic sodium salts during fusion with sodium metal."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The blood-red that is not a mistake*** — a compound containing both N and S gives NaSCN on fusion; with Fe3+ it turns blood red instead of Prussian blue — and that red colour is the positive proof of both elements at once.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Making the Invisible Detectable Carbon and hydrogen reveal themselves by simple combustion tests, but **nitrogen, sulphur and halogens** hide inside covalent molecules where ionic reagents cannot touch them. **Lassaigne's test** (sodium fusion) solves this by converting every covalent N, S and X into **ions** (CN⁻, S²⁻, X⁻) in one operation — then classic inorganic tests finish the job.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Why sodium fusion is needed - In an organic molecule, N, S and halogens are held in **covalent bonds**; the usual ionic precipitation tests fail. - Fusing the compound with **molten sodium** converts them to **ionic sodium salts**: **NaCN** (from N), **Na₂S** (from S), **NaX** (from halogen).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Extract recipe: Na fusion red-hot -> water -> boil -> filter. N = Prussian blue; S = violet (nitroprusside) or black PbS; X = AgNO3 colours white/pale-yellow/yellow with NH4OH solubility test; N+S = blood red NaSCN.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Describe Lassaigne's test for the detection of nitrogen in an organic compound.** — A small piece of **sodium metal** is heated with a little of the organic compound in a fusion tube until **red hot**, then plunged into distilled water, boiled and filtered.…  ·  **NEB-style (3m): How are sulphur and halogens detected using Lassaigne's extract?** — **Sulphur:** (i) extract + **sodium nitroprusside** → **violet colour** (Na₄[Fe(CN)₅NOS]) confirms sulphur; (ii) extract + **acetic acid, then lead acetate** → **black precipitate of PbS** confirms sulphur.…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The whole test is one idea: convert covalent to ionic, then let textbook inorganic chemistry do the rest — sodium fusion is the bridge between the two chemistries.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Lassaigne's test: fuse organic compound with Na metal red-hot -> drop in water, boil, filter = Lassaigne's extract (NaCN, Na2S, NaX). Nitrogen: extract + FeSO4 + NaOH, boil (Na4[Fe(CN)6]), acidify H2SO4 + Fe3+ -> Prussian blue Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Prussian blue, the nitrogen confirmatory precipitate, is the same pigment that 18th-century artists ground into paint — analytical chemistry and art history share one formula.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain the blood-red colour obtained when both N and S are present.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **The blood-red colour is not a failure:** when N and S are both present, Prussian blue cannot form; the red Fe(SCN)₃ is the *correct* positive result for both elements.  ·  **HNO₃ boiling is not optional:** skipping it leaves CN⁻/S²⁻ to form AgCN/Ag₂S, muddying the halogen colours.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Flame/combustion tests detect C and H, not N/S/X:** C and H need no fusion (CO₂ turns lime water milky; H₂O condenses on a cold surface) — only N, S, X need the extract.  ·  ## 7.
